newsitem.title: USA: Costs chew up travel budgets.
newsitem.headline: Costs chew up travel budgets.

text.p: Airfare and hotel prices, the two major cost components of most business travel, are causing some sticker shock in corporate circles.

A recent report compiled by American Express shows that business airfares rose for the sixth month in a row -- with the typical cost of a business traveler's ticket at the highest level since January of 1992.

At the same time a report from Horwath Hospitality Consulting and Smith Travel Research projects that hotel rooms will be hard to get and expensive in almost every major market through the end of the year.

New York, Boston, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Orlando are among the cities which have seen sighificant jumps in hotel room prices and occupancy rates this year, according to Jeff Marvel, director of the Horwath Hospitality Consulting.

The hotel situation is a result of demand finally catching up with what had been an over-supply of rooms. Marvel said in an interview that the latest findings did show some occupancy rates dropping for the first time in 54 months.
"So the industry is maybe peaking in terms of occupancy growth," he said.

The industry is adding rooms, Marvel said, but the trend has been toward limited service, extended stay properties not typically located in city centres. Such hotels tend to be suburban or airport oriented because they often cater to people who are being relocated by their employer, he said.
Meanwhile the Travel Industry Association of America in its annual autumn travel forecast -- based on a survey of 1,500 adults -- found that business travel appears to be levelling off.
The number of people surveyed who thought they'd likely be travelling on business during the rest of 1996 dropped to the lowest level since the group began tracking such trends five years ago.

The group said the situation comes from a "cautious corporate climate" where executives have an eye on holding down expenses. Another factor is that in companies that have slimmed down their structure the remaining executives have had to take on more travel already and they already have full schedules.

Figures for the past few years indicate that the amount of business travel is about the same but that fewer people are making the trips. Travel has probably reached a plateau, an association spokeswoman said, because those who are doing the travel are getting burned out and can't take on more.

On another front Delta Airlines last month began testing live television via satellite in one of its Boeing 767s. The system shows four cabel channels -- CNN, comedy, sports and variety -- on domestic U.S. flights.
The programmes are shown on the screens usually used for movies -- one in first class and two in coach. But the flight attendants and not the passengers control the channels.
The six-month test is designed to determine if such programming is viable on a larger scale, a Delta spokesman said.

So far, he said, passenger reaction has been "quite positive" and even involved -- one flight attendant tried to change the channel during coverage of the Republican National Convention in San Diego and had to switch it back after the passengers complained.
United Airlines also has its eye on entertainment.

The carrier says it will be changing the movies offered on longer flights every two weeks instead of once a month, and will add several TV situation comedies -- Seinfeld, Frasier, Friends, Home Improvement, Mad About You, The John Larroquette Show and Wings -- to its video programmes beginning in October.
